citations.anchor: leaves relations out when they are not asked for
citations.why: With relations off the author record is absent from the document, yet the surviving reference still carries $key {email: 'ada@x.test'} — a key only the identity-column projection over the unwalked neighbour can produce, and the assertion fails if the reference falls back to the foreign row id.

citations.anchor: leads with the envelope and skips the inverse relation
citations.why: csvColumns(post) is asserted to equal an exact list that omits the inverse relation 'backlinks' while keeping the owning 'related'. Only the CSV-column clause is pinned; that the inverse side is left out of the export document and not written on import is not asserted anywhere.

citations.anchor: dry-runs without writing, and says what it would do
citations.why: After POSTing the document to /import/preview the entry list is asserted to still have the same length as before the call, so a preview that wrote a row fails. The 'not one byte' half (no asset blob uploaded by a dry run) is not asserted — the suite exercises no media.

citations.anchor: round-trips a graph: export, wipe, import, and it is back
citations.why: After the import it asserts text, number and select all survived — the regression named in the test's own comment, where the relation pass resent a partial value bag and blanked every field it omitted. It then reads both histories back and asserts one revision each: the author is written first, so the article's link lands with its values and the link pass must find nothing to do. Pins the first clause and the no-second-revision half of the second.

citations.anchor: keeps the two policies apart: duplicate the record, link its author
citations.why: policy=duplicate with the default relation policy yields two articles and exactly one author, still the original row — if ConflictPolicy reached depth 1 a second author would appear.

citations.anchor: links a related record that is already here instead of adding another
citations.why: The matched author is asserted to be verdict skip/relation-linked, to still be the single original row id, and to be what the new article points at — a link that wrote to the related entry would change its verdict or add a row. That its field values are left byte-for-byte untouched is not separately asserted.

citations.anchor: round-trips a graph: export, wipe, import, and it is back
citations.why: Pins the other half: with both records wiped the default link policy has nothing to link to, and the author is asserted to come back as a created row.

citations.anchor: links a related record that is already here instead of adding another
citations.why: The author's verdict is skip, and the imported article is then read back and asserted to have values.author === the skipped author's id — so a skipped entry that fell out of the id map would leave the relation unresolved and fail this.

citations.anchor: does not index an empty key
citations.why: remember() with an empty key, then resolve() by an empty key, is asserted to report Unresolved — indexing the keyless record would return its target id here.

citations.anchor: separates two locales of the same key
citations.why: keyFingerprint('article', {slug:'hello'}, 'en') is asserted not to equal the 'de' fingerprint; dropping the locale from the fingerprint collapses them into one match.

citations.anchor: cannot be forged by a value containing the separator
citations.why: Two key bags that a separator-joined encoding would render identically are asserted to fingerprint differently — the assertion only holds under a JSON encoding.

citations.anchor: never writes across workspaces, whatever the manifest claims
citations.why: The manifest's sourceWorkspaceId is hand-edited to a second workspace the caller also belongs to; the forged record is asserted to land in the request's workspace and the other workspace is asserted to hold nothing.

citations.anchor: hides a content type the workspace was never granted
citations.why: An export against a workspace with no content grants is asserted to answer 404 for a type that does exist — a 403 or any other status would leak that the type is there.

citations.anchor: refuses more entries than the limit before reading any of them
citations.why: readZipDirectory alone (no readZipEntry call) is asserted to throw on the entry count, which is the 'counts rejected from the central directory, before decompression' clause.

citations.anchor: refuses an entry declaring more than the per-entry ceiling
citations.why: The sizes clause: readZipDirectory throws on the declared uncompressed size against maxArchiveEntryBytes, again before any member is unpacked.

citations.anchor: refuses an archive whose compression ratio is not real content
citations.why: The ratio clause: a 4 MB zero-filled member is rejected by readZipDirectory with /compressed far beyond/ without being decompressed.

citations.anchor: refuses a path that climbs out of the archive
citations.why: A forged '../' member name makes readZipDirectory throw rather than return a normalised path — sanitising instead of refusing would return an entry and fail the toThrow.

citations.anchor: refuses a document written by a newer format version
citations.why: manifest.version = 99 is asserted to give 400 with a /newer version/i message rather than a best-effort read.

citations.anchor: does not reconstruct media — a filename in a cell is not a file
citations.why: A row round-tripped through recordToRow/rowToRecord is asserted to come back with media === [], so a populated media cell can never become an asset reference.

citations.anchor: rejects an empty selection
citations.why: POST /export with ids: [] is asserted to answer 400 — an 'empty means everything' reading would answer 200.

citations.anchor: counts but does not upload during a dry run
citations.why: Pins the clause the e2e citation's own note says it cannot: `dryRun: true` is asserted to leave the fake uploader untouched and the run's rollback list empty, while `assetsNew` still counts the upload it would have made. A dry run that reached UploadAssetUseCase would put bytes in the bucket and fail here.

citations.anchor: previews the very verdicts the apply then delivers
citations.why: One file is POSTed to /import/preview and then to /import with the same policy, and the two runs' verdicts are compared as (type, id, action, reason) tuples plus counts. The fixture is built so the run holds all four actions at once — a matched article (update), a purged one (create), a linked author (skip) and a record naming a type this installation lacks (error) — and that set is asserted before the comparison, so parity over a document that could only ever skip cannot pass for the invariant.

citations.anchor: rebuilds a cycle the file cannot have ordered
citations.why: test_page is the only self-referential fixture, so alpha.parent = beta and beta.parent = alpha is a genuine cycle: both are exported as roots (asserted $depth [0, 0], so the importer's depth sort cannot re-impose an order), the rows are deleted, the document's records are reversed, and both links are asserted after the import. No single-pass write order satisfies both — dropping the applyLinks pass leaves whichever row went first pointing at null.

citations.anchor: matches on the natural key before the source row id
citations.why: Ada's exported record is hand-edited to claim Bob's row id, so both lookups hit at once — byKey names Ada, bySourceId names Bob — and only the order decides. The verdict's targetId is asserted to be Ada and Bob's name/email are read back unchanged; swapping the `??` operands in `run` overwrites Bob with Ada and fails both.

citations.anchor: keys on the identity the manifest recorded
citations.why: Pins the second clause. The manifest's identity for test_author is asserted to be ['email'] as derived here, then rewritten to ['name'] while the record's email is changed to one nothing holds and its $id to a uuid nothing holds. The record must still match Ada by name. Either side of the fingerprint re-deriving locally keys on email, misses, and creates a second Ada.

citations.anchor: locale twins in one translation group
citations.why: An en/de pair is exported with locales: true (both rows and one shared $localeGroup asserted in the document), then imported under policy=duplicate so both rows are written fresh. The two created verdicts' rows are read back and asserted to share one localeGroupId that is not the source group — a create that ignored the sibling's group gives each copy a group of its own.

citations.anchor: will not create what the caller could not have created by hand
citations.why: A role holding content:read + content:import and nothing else (seedUserWithPermissions, so no shipped role's permission set can hide the split) imports a document whose one record was purged first, so the only thing it can ask for is a create. counts.create is 0, the verdict is error/forbidden, and the type is asserted empty afterwards.

citations.anchor: checks the permission the record
citations.why: The other half, and the one that makes the check per-action rather than per-caller: the role holds content:create but not content:update, and the file matches a live row under policy=update. The live row's `number` was moved to 99 after the export, so a write that got through would be visible; it is asserted still 99, with counts.update 0 and an error/forbidden verdict.

citations.anchor: leaves the inverse side of a two-way relation out of the document
citations.why: Closes the export clause the flatten.spec citation could not reach. An article is tagged, the owning export is asserted to carry relations.tags (so the fixture is a real link and not an absent one), and the export rooted at the tag is asserted to hold one record with no `articles` key in relations or values — a walk that followed the inverse side would put the article in the tag's document.

citations.anchor: links a related record without writing a word to it
citations.why: Closes the clause the other two I-15 citations left open. The live author is renamed after the export, so the file and the row differ on `name` while still sharing the `email` the key matches on; after the import the author is asserted to still read 'Ada Lovelace' rather than the file's 'Ada'. A `link` that also wrote the file's values would keep the same row id and the same skip verdict and pass everything else.

citations.anchor: spends one write per record, and a second only where a link could not resolve on the first
citations.why: The two-page cycle is the one document holding both halves at once: whichever page is written first cannot resolve its parent and genuinely needs the link pass, while the second one's parent is already in the id map. Both parent links are asserted rebuilt — so a link pass that never fires fails here rather than passing a bare revision count — and the two revision totals are asserted to be [1, 2]: exactly one second write across the two rows. Before the guard was fixed this read [2, 2]; with the pass disabled it reads [1, 1] and the parent assertions fall first.

citations.anchor: a different file retires the verdicts of the last one
citations.why: The two files answer with different verdicts, so the assertion is not only that the table vanished: after picking the second file the table is asserted gone, the Import button gone and the dialog back on 'Check the file' — then a second check is asserted to name the *second* file's record and no longer the first's. A dialog that kept the first preview would show one file's verdicts above another file's Import button and fail on the first assertion.

citations.anchor: changing what happens to a matching record retires the verdicts
citations.why: The conflict-policy half. With verdicts on screen, selecting 'Update it with the file's values' is asserted to leave no table and no Import button, and the re-check is asserted to reach the server with policy=update (read out of the multipart body) — so a dialog that kept the skip-time table, or one that re-rendered it without re-running, fails.

citations.anchor: changing what happens to the records the file links to retires them too
citations.why: The relation-policy half — the clause a single `onChange` on the first question would leave unguarded. Selecting 'Add them again as new records' retires the table, and the re-check is asserted to carry relations=recreate with policy still skip, so the two answers are shown to be independent as well as both invalidating.

citations.anchor: an import re-reads the collection it wrote into
citations.why: The row set the entries mock serves is mutable and the apply handler pushes the imported record into it, so the record exists on the server the instant the apply answers and the *only* path to the screen is the refresh pass. The row is asserted absent before and visible after, with no reload — which is exactly the shipped defect (`invalidateQueries(['content'])` matched none of the library's roots, so the toast said 'imported' and the table never moved). Only the collection's own type is pinned here; see the `partial` below for the two clauses a browser cannot observe.

citations.anchor: offers file bytes only in a format that can carry them
citations.why: Closes the interface half the export-entries citation could not reach. The Files toggle is asserted enabled and checked on ZIP, then disabled *and reading as unchecked* on JSON, JSON Lines and CSV in turn, and enabled again on the way back to ZIP — all four formats, so a dialog that special-cased the lossy one would leave Files live for JSON. Every preflight request the dialog sent is then asserted to carry `depth.media === (format === 'zip')`, which is the difference between disabling the toggle and greying it out while still asking the server for bytes.
